## Overview

Kumyks are a Turkic ethnic group living in Dagestan, Chechnya and North Ossetia. Their traditional territory includes the Kumyk Plateau, northern Dagestan, northeastern Chechnya, lands bordering the Caspian Sea, areas in North Ossetia, and the banks of the Terek River. Territories historically populated by Kumyks and associated with their former state entities are called Kumykia. Kumyks are the largest Turkic people in the North Caucasus, the third-largest ethnic group of Dagestan, and the second-largest Turkic-speaking ethnic group in the Caucasus after Azerbaijanis. According to the Russian national census of 2010, more than 500,000 Kumyks lived in Russia. Their language belongs to the Kipchak-Cuman subfamily of the Turkic languages and historically served as a lingua franca across much of the Northern Caucasus.

## Material culture

### Architecture

The sources identify Tarki as the historical capital of the Shamkhalate and mention Kumyk settlements and auls.

## Music & performance

The sources do record a literary and theatrical context for the Kumyk language: Temirbolat Biybolatov is described as a Kumyk poet, writer, translator, and theatre figure, and the first regular Kumyk newspapers and magazines appeared in 1917–18 under his editorship.

## Dance & theatre

They identify Temirbolat Biybolatov as a theatre figure and state that the Kumyk language appears in literary works by Leo Tolstoy, Mikhail Lermontov, and Bestuzhev-Marlinsky.

## Festivals & rituals

They do record religious and political changes: some early Kipchaks associated with Kumyk history were Tengrists, Christians, or irreligious, while later Kipchaks were Islamised. The sources also describe Kumyks as participating in the religious and political history of the Caucasus.

## Foodways

The historical sources mention Kumyk bread and cattle in descriptions of warfare and plundering, but these references do not describe Kumyk foodways.

## Oral tradition & literature

Kumyk verbal tradition is described as having carried some proverbs and sayings from the period of the Khazar Kaghanate. The sources state that Kumyks have diverse and disputed origins, with proposed connections to Khazars, Kipchaks, Cumans, other Turks of the early Middle Ages, and pre-Turkic populations. They also record the historical importance of the Cuman language as the literary culture of Kumyks and the wider region of Dagestan, the North Caucasus, and Southern Ukraine.

Irchi Kazak, also written Ийрчы Къазакъ and Yırçı Qazaq, born in 1839, is described as usually considered the greatest poet of the Kumyk language. The first regular Kumyk newspapers and magazines appeared in 1917–18 under the editorship of Temirbolat Biybolatov. The newspaper Ёлдаш, or Yoldash, meaning “Companion,” succeeded the Soviet-era Ленин ёлу, or Lenin yolu, meaning “Lenin’s Path,” and prints around 5,000 copies three times a week. The Kumyk language also appears in works including Tolstoy’s “The Raid,” The Cossacks, and Hadji Murat; Lermontov’s A Hero of Our Time; and Bestuzhev-Marlinsky’s “Molla-nur” and “Ammalat-bek.”

## Language & religion

Kumyk is a Turkic language belonging to the Kipchak-Cuman subfamily of the Kipchak family. The sources describe it as a descendant of Cuman, with likely influence from Khazar, and with words from the Bulghar and Oghuz substratum. Its closest languages are identified as Karachay-Balkar, Crimean Tatar, and Karaim. Dialects named in the sources include Kaitag, Terek, Buynaksk, and Xasavyurt; the latter two became the basis of the literary language.

Kumyk served as a lingua franca across much of the Northern Caucasus until the 1930s and was an official language of communication between North-Eastern Caucasian nations and the Russian administration. In 1923 it was declared the state language of Dagestan ASSR. Kumyk was written in Arabic script, with the oldest recorded use dating to the mid-17th century; a Latin alphabet was officially adopted in 1928, and a Cyrillic alphabet in 1938. The sources describe Islamisation among later Kipchaks.
